title: Niongoze Fellowship 2026: Leadership, Mentorship and Training Opportunity for Young Tanzanian Women
summary: Applications are officially open for the Niongoze Fellowship Class of 2026 , Doyenne Tanzania’s flagship leadership development programme for young Tanzanian women who want to strengthen their confidence, develop practical leadership skills and become part of a community of purpose-driven changemakers. The 2026 application window runs from: 1 September 2026 to 25 September 2026 The official Doyenne Tanzania website specifies that applications close on: 25 September 2026 at 23:59 East Africa Time (EAT). The Niongoze Fellowship is designed around Doyenne Tanzania’s broader mission of building a generation of qualified female leaders through leadership training, mentorship, coaching and empowerment . Doyenne describes the Fellowship as its flagship programme for equipping university students with transformative leadership skills. The programme is particularly relevant for young women who want to become more confident leaders, develop the skills needed to influence their communities, learn directly from experienced leaders and connect with other ambitious young women across Tanzania. Official website and application access: Doyenne Tanzania – Niongoze Fellowship 2026 About the Niongoze Fellowship The Niongoze Fellowship is a leadership development initiative created by Doyenne Tanzania , a Tanzanian nonprofit organization dedicated to expanding leadership opportunities for girls and young women. Doyenne describes itself as an organization committed to developing qualified female leaders through: Leadership training Mentorship Coaching Empowerment Professional and personal development Its wider vision is a community in which girls and women have equal opportunities to lead. The Niongoze Fellowship sits at the centre of that mission. Rather than focusing only on academic performance, the programme seeks to help young women understand leadership at a more personal and practical level: how they see themselves, how they work with other people, how they participate in organizations and how they create positive change in their communities. What Does “Niongoze” Mean for the Programme? The Fellowship is structured as a leadership journey rather than a one-off workshop. Historically, Doyenne has described Niongoze as an annual programme combining: Leadership training Mentoring Coaching Peer learning In-person activities Virtual activities Independent descriptions of the programme have characterized it as a year-long leadership development initiative in Tanzania, while Doyenne’s current website describes Niongoze as its flagship programme for university students. The overall objective is to help young women develop the knowledge, confidence and relationships needed to take increasingly meaningful leadership roles. Who Is the Niongoze Fellowship Designed For? For the 2026 application cycle, Doyenne’s official website asks: “Are you a young Tanzanian woman ready to grow in confidence, strengthen your leadership skills, and join a community of purpose-driven changemakers?” The current website also describes the Niongoze Fellowship as: A flagship leadership programme that equips university students with transformative skills. This makes the opportunity especially relevant to young Tanzanian women currently building their leadership experience while pursuing higher education. Potential applicants may include women involved in: Student government University associations Community organizations Volunteer initiatives Youth programmes Social-impact projects Advocacy STEM initiatives Entrepreneurship Health programmes Environmental initiatives Civil society activities Professional associations However, holding a formal leadership title should not automatically be assumed to be a requirement unless the application form explicitly says so. What Does the Fellowship Aim to Develop? Doyenne’s broader programme model emphasizes several interconnected dimensions of leadership. Historical descriptions of Niongoze highlight themes such as: Leadership Confidence Resilience Wellbeing and developing leadership understanding at: Individual level Group level Community level These areas are important because effective leadership involves more than holding a title. The Fellowship seeks to develop young women who can understand themselves, collaborate effectively and contribute meaningfully to the people and institutions around them. Personal Leadership The Fellowship has historically begun by focusing on: Leadership of self. This may involve areas such as: Self-awareness Confidence Personal values Decision-making Goal-setting Resilience Communication Understanding strengths Reflecting on personal growth Doyenne’s 2024 Fellowship page, for example, describes the first colloquium as focusing on personal leadership training . The idea is that leadership begins with understanding one’s own values, abilities and responsibilities. Group Leadership Another dimension concerns leadership within teams and organizations. Previous Niongoze programme structures have included training at the: Group level. Relevant skills can include: Communication Teamwork Collaboration Conflict management Listening Delegation Relationship-building Working across differences Collective decision-making These skills are particularly useful for university students who are already involved in clubs, associations, community initiatives or student leadership. Community Leadership The Fellowship also extends leadership beyond the individual and group level toward: Community leadership. Past programme descriptions include a dedicated community leadership component. This helps participants think about questions such as: What problems affect my community? How can young women contribute to solutions? How can leaders mobilize other people? How do we create sustainable impact? How can leadership strengthen inclusion and participation? This community orientation helps distinguish leadership development from purely personal career coaching. Confidence Development Confidence is a major theme of Doyenne’s work. Its current website presents the 2026 opportunity as a chance for young Tanzanian women to: Grow in confidence while building leadership capacity. For many emerging leaders, confidence can affect their willingness to: Speak publicly Express ideas Apply for opportunities Lead teams Challenge established practices Participate in decision-making Advocate for communities The Fellowship therefore seeks to create an environment where young women can develop both competence and the confidence to use it. Mentorship Mentorship forms another important part of Doyenne’s overall leadership model. Doyenne explains that its programmes connect girls with: Leaders Mentors Changemakers so participants can learn from people who have already travelled similar leadership paths. Mentorship can help emerging leaders understand: Career decisions Leadership challenges Professional development Personal growth Networking Navigating institutional environments For university students, having access to experienced female leaders may be particularly valuable when making decisions about postgraduate study, employment, entrepreneurship, public service or community leadership. Coaching and Leadership Development Doyenne also identifies coaching as part of its broader organizational approach. Coaching differs slightly from mentorship. Where mentorship often involves learning from someone’s experience, coaching can focus more directly on helping a participant: Clarify goals Recognize strengths Identify barriers Develop action plans Reflect on progress Improve leadership behaviors Taken together, leadership training, mentoring and coaching can provide participants with a broader development experience than a single short workshop. A Community of Young Female Leaders One of the strongest features of the Niongoze Fellowship is the opportunity to join a community of other young women interested in leadership. The current call specifically emphasizes joining a: “community of purpose-driven changemakers.” Peer networks can be valuable because participants may continue to support each other long after formal programme activities conclude. Fellows may come from different: Universities Academic disciplines Regions Leadership backgrounds Professional interests but share an interest in creating positive change. Previous Niongoze Fellows Have Come From Diverse Academic Fields The Niongoze Fellowship is not limited to a single academic discipline. The 2024 cohort profiled by Doyenne included young women studying areas such as: Political Science and Public Administration Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering Cybersecurity and Digital Forensics Electrical Engineering Medicine International Relations and Diplomacy Law Accounting and Finance Tourism Management Social Work This indicates that leadership development is intended to cut across academic and professional fields. A woman studying medicine may want to become a health leader. A law student may want to advance justice. An engineering student may want to lead in technology. A tourism student may want to champion sustainable development. The Fellowship provides a shared leadership platform across these different aspirations. Previous Fellows Have Represented Universities Across Tanzania Past Niongoze participants have come from institutions including: University of Dar es Salaam University of Dodoma Mzumbe University Hubert Kairuki Memorial University St. Augustine University of Tanzania College of African Wildlife Management Kilimanjaro Christian Medical University College Dar es Salaam Institute of Technology Dr. Salim Ahmed Salim Centre for Foreign Relations among others. The Fellowship therefore creates opportunities for networking beyond a participant’s own campus. Leadership Beyond Academic Achievement The profiles of previous Fellows also demonstrate that Doyenne looks broadly at leadership potential. Past participants have been involved in: Student government Health outreach Women’s empowerment STEM advocacy Child-rights advocacy Technology initiatives Conservation Environmental projects Community organizations Entrepreneurship Public speaking Student clubs Volunteer work This suggests that applicants should think about leadership as something broader than academic grades. Leadership can be demonstrated by: Starting an initiative Volunteering Representing students Solving a community problem Organizing a project Supporting peers Advocating for change Taking responsibility Leadership Training Through Colloquia Previous editions of the Fellowship have used a series of: Colloquia to structure leadership learning. Doyenne’s 2024 programme description identifies: A first colloquium on personal leadership A second colloquium focusing on leadership at the group level A third colloquium focusing on community leadership Graduation as the concluding stage Another description of Doyenne’s programme similarly notes an annual series of four colloquia delivered through physical and virtual formats. Applicants should note, however, that Doyenne’s current public 2026 homepage does not publish the complete 2026 schedule. Participants should therefore rely on the application materials or Doyenne directly for the final Class of 2026 timetable. In-Person and Virtual Learning Past Niongoze Fellowship programmes have combined: Physical activities Virtual activities rather than operating entirely online. This allows Fellows to benefit from face-to-face networking while also participating in learning and mentoring across geographic distances. The exact delivery format for the Class of 2026 should be confirmed through the application process because Doyenne’s current homepage does not publicly list every session format. Is There a Fellowship Fee or Stipend? The current 2026 Doyenne website does not publicly specify a stipend, cash award, travel allowance or financial benefit for selected Fellows. Older Doyenne communications have described participation in earlier cohorts as free, but applicants should not assume that every cost or financial arrangement is identical for the 2026 class unless this is confirmed in the current application materials. For publication accuracy, the Niongoze Fellowship 2026 should therefore not be advertised as a funded or fully funded fellowship unless Doyenne issues current 2026 financial details confirming this. Application Period Applications opened on: 1 September 2026 and close on: 25 September 2026. Doyenne’s official website provides the more precise closing time: 25 September 2026 at 23:59 EAT. Applicants should aim to submit before the final evening rather than waiting until the deadline. How to Apply Applications are available through the official Doyenne Tanzania website. Apply through Doyenne Tanzania The homepage currently displays the “Apply for the Class of 2026” option for the Niongoze Fellowship. Applicants should follow the official application link provided there. Contact Doyenne Tanzania The organization lists the following contact information: Email: info@doyenne.or.tz Phone: +255 757 019 087 Candidates with questions about: Eligibility Programme schedule Required documents Participation costs University status Application form issues should contact Doyenne directly if the information is not covered in the current application form. Application Information Session Doyenne also announced a Niongoze Fellowship information session and live Q A for 10 September 2026, reflecting its effort to help applicants understand the programme and application process. Applicants who missed that session should use the official website and Doyenne contact channels for any remaining questions. How to Prepare a Strong Niongoze Fellowship Application 1. Explain Why Leadership Matters to You Avoid simply writing that you “want to become a leader.” Explain: What type of leader you want to become Who you want to serve What problem you care about What change you hope to create A clear leadership purpose is more persuasive than a generic interest in professional development. 2. Show Leadership Through Action You do not necessarily need a prestigious title. Think about examples where you have: Organized people Solved a problem Supported classmates Volunteered Started a project Advocated for others Taken responsibility Helped your community Leadership potential often appears through action rather than formal titles. 3. Be Honest About What You Still Need to Learn A fellowship exists because applicants are still developing. You can explain that you want to improve areas such as: Public speaking Confidence Decision-making Team leadership Networking Resilience Strategic thinking Showing self-awareness can strengthen a leadership application. 4. Connect Your Leadership Goals to Tanzania The Fellowship is explicitly focused on developing young Tanzanian women. Explain how stronger leadership skills could help you contribute to: Your university Your professional field Your local community Tanzania more broadly 5. Demonstrate Community Orientation Doyenne’s Fellowship has historically moved from personal leadership to group and community leadership. A strong applicant should therefore think beyond individual career advancement. Consider: Who benefits if I become a stronger leader? That question can help shape a meaningful application. 6. Explain Why Niongoze Specifically Rather than applying because “it is a good opportunity,” explain why you value elements such as: Mentorship Leadership training Coaching Female leadership networks Learning from accomplished women Peer community This demonstrates that you understand the programme. Important Details at a Glance Programme: Niongoze Fellowship Class of 2026 Organization: Doyenne Tanzania Country: Tanzania Target group: Young Tanzanian women Current programme description: Flagship leadership programme for university students Focus: Leadership development Core approaches: Training, mentorship, coaching and empowerment Application opening: 1 September 2026 Application deadline: 25 September 2026 Closing time: 23:59 EAT Official website: www.doyenne.or.tz Email: info@doyenne.or.tz Phone: +255 757 019 087 Important Note on Age and Detailed Eligibility Previous external descriptions of Niongoze have characterized the broader programme as serving young women around 17–25 years old . However, Doyenne’s current 2026 public website does not publish a specific age range on the application announcement . It instead describes applicants as young Tanzanian women and describes Niongoze as a flagship programme for university students. For accuracy, applicants should therefore check the current 2026 application form before relying on a historical age threshold. Conclusion The Niongoze Fellowship 2026 is an important leadership development opportunity for young Tanzanian women who want to strengthen their confidence, develop practical leadership skills and connect with an ambitious community of female changemakers. Organized by Doyenne Tanzania , the Fellowship forms part of the organization’s mission to build a generation of qualified female leaders through training, mentorship, coaching and empowerment . The current Doyenne website identifies Niongoze as its flagship programme for university students. Previous cohorts demonstrate the interdisciplinary nature of the programme, bringing together women studying fields ranging from medicine and law to engineering, international relations, cybersecurity, accounting and tourism. Historically, the Fellowship has explored leadership at the personal, group and community levels and has combined physical and virtual learning experiences. For a young Tanzanian woman who wants to become more confident, develop her leadership identity, learn from mentors and build relationships with other emerging leaders, Niongoze offers a structured pathway for personal and community-oriented growth. Applications for the Class of 2026 opened on 1 September 2026 and close on: 25 September 2026 at 23:59 EAT. title: EU No Child Left Behind Grant 2026: Up to €1 Million for NGOs Supporting Children with Disabilities in Egypt
summary: The European Union has opened a major new call for proposals titled “No Child Left Behind: Inclusion and Protection for Children with Disabilities” , inviting eligible nonprofit organisations to develop projects that advance the rights, protection, participation and well-being of children with disabilities in Egypt. Published under reference EuropeAid/186723/DD/ACT/EG , the opportunity is designed to strengthen the environments in which children with disabilities live, learn and participate. It combines a rights-based approach to disability with practical interventions around child protection, inclusive education, community participation, family support, accessibility, social protection and institutional capacity. The EU Delegation to Egypt has confirmed that eligible NGOs are invited to apply and that the deadline is 30 September 2026 . The call has three major priority areas: Human rights and protection of children with disabilities Social inclusion and participation Family and enabling environments Applicants must address at least one of these priority areas, although proposals integrating more than one priority will be viewed particularly favourably during evaluation. Detailed call information reproduced by funding databases indicates an overall budget of approximately €3.9 million , with individual grants ranging from €650,000 to €1 million and projects generally lasting 24 to 36 months . Funding is reported to cover between 51% and 95% of eligible project costs , meaning most applicants will need to demonstrate an appropriate financing structure for the balance where the EU grant does not cover the full budget. A particularly important feature of the call is its emphasis on strengthening local organisations. At least 60% of eligible action costs is reported to be intended for financial support to third parties, such as Egyptian civil society organisations, community-based organisations and organisations of persons with disabilities. The normal maximum amount of support per third-party recipient is reported as €60,000 , unless a higher amount can be appropriately justified. The deadline for submission is: 30 September 2026 Applicants should consult the official EU Funding Tenders/EuropeAid documentation referenced by the EU Delegation to Egypt before submitting, since the full guidelines govern eligibility, partnership structure, budget rules, documentation and application procedure. View the EU Medbridge opportunity page About the No Child Left Behind Call for Proposals The programme responds to continuing gaps in the realisation of children’s rights in Egypt, particularly for children affected by overlapping disadvantages such as disability, poverty, social exclusion, geographic isolation and limited access to appropriate services. Egypt ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1990 , and its 2014 Constitution affirms the state’s commitment to protecting children. National policies have subsequently sought to improve education, health and child-protection outcomes. Nevertheless, children with disabilities continue to experience barriers that can affect their ability to participate fully in family, school and community life. The call therefore moves beyond a narrow service-delivery model. Its overall objective is to contribute to the full realisation of the: Rights Dignity Well-being Participation Equality of children with disabilities in Egypt. It aims to achieve this by supporting inclusive social environments, strengthening families and communities, and improving the institutional and systemic capacity needed to deliver accessible and equitable services. Why This Funding Opportunity Matters Children with disabilities can experience disadvantages at several different levels simultaneously. These can include: Discrimination within families or communities Exclusion from schools Violence or neglect Limited access to health and social services Stigma Inaccessible public spaces Limited participation in community activities Barriers to social protection Insufficient family support Lack of opportunities to express their views The programme is therefore deliberately broad. It recognizes that inclusion cannot be achieved by concentrating only on the child as an individual. Effective disability inclusion also depends on: Parents Caregivers Schools Health workers Community organisations Religious and community leaders Government services Social-protection systems Accessible physical environments Public attitudes The call is designed to support interventions capable of working across those interconnected levels. Global Objective of the Call The programme’s global objective is to contribute to the: Full realisation of the rights, dignity and well-being of children with disabilities in Egypt. It intends to do so by: Promoting inclusive social environments Strengthening families Strengthening communities Improving institutional capacity Improving systemic capacity Expanding access to equitable services Expanding access to accessible services This makes the call relevant to organisations working in both direct service delivery and systems change. Specific Objective 1: Protecting the Rights of Children With Disabilities The first specific objective seeks to promote a: Rights-based approach to disability and child protection. The programme aims to protect children with disabilities from: Discrimination Neglect Violence Abuse while promoting equality. This framing is important because disability programmes can sometimes treat beneficiaries only as recipients of care. The EU call instead emphasizes children with disabilities as rights-holders . That approach can involve ensuring children and their families understand: Their legal rights Available services Social-protection entitlements Mechanisms for reporting abuse Available support systems It also means institutions and communities should understand their responsibility to respect and uphold those rights. Specific Objective 2: Inclusion and Participation The second objective is focused on ensuring that children with disabilities can participate meaningfully in: School Peer groups Community life It also aims to challenge: Stigma Harmful social norms Discriminatory attitudes that restrict children’s development, participation or voice. Participation should therefore not be interpreted simply as physical presence. A child may technically attend school but still be excluded from learning, friendships, recreation or decision-making. Meaningful inclusion involves enabling children to: Participate Communicate Learn Play Build friendships Develop skills Express opinions Influence decisions affecting their lives Specific Objective 3: Strengthening Families and Caregivers The third objective recognizes the critical role played by: Parents Caregivers Families Community actors in enabling children with disabilities to thrive. The programme seeks to strengthen their capacity while supporting family- and community-based environments that promote the child’s: Development Well-being Inclusion Participation This can involve practical caregiving support as well as: Counselling Training Peer support Financial resilience Links to social protection Community rehabilitation Priority Area 1: Human Rights and Protection of Children With Disabilities The first priority focuses on protecting children with disabilities from harm while ensuring equal treatment. Eligible or relevant activities may include promoting: Non-discrimination and equality within: Families Schools Communities This could potentially involve: Rights-awareness campaigns Community dialogue Training for teachers Child-protection mechanisms Referral systems Strengthening safeguarding practices The call is not limited to these examples, but proposed activities should clearly contribute to the programme objectives. Preventing Violence, Neglect, Abuse and Exploitation Projects under Priority Area 1 may work to prevent and respond to: Violence Neglect Abuse Exploitation affecting children with disabilities. The call specifically includes the promotion of: Positive parenting and non-violent discipline within families. This can be particularly important because children with disabilities may face heightened protection risks while also experiencing barriers to reporting mistreatment. Strong proposals might therefore combine: Prevention Awareness Identification Referral Response Family support rather than focusing only on awareness campaigns. Building the Capacity of Frontline Community Actors The call also highlights the importance of increasing awareness among frontline actors such as: Teachers Religious leaders Health workers Community volunteers These groups frequently interact with children and families and can play a central role in recognizing: Abuse Exclusion Service needs Protection risks Projects may therefore strengthen their ability to understand and uphold the rights of children with disabilities. Helping Families Access Integrated Service Cards Another possible intervention is helping children with disabilities and their families obtain: Integrated service cards and understand the rights and entitlements associated with them. This illustrates the practical nature of the call. A rights-based programme is not only about advocacy at national level. It can also help individual families navigate administrative systems and access benefits for which they are already eligible. Priority Area 2: Social Inclusion and Participation The second priority addresses the barriers that keep children with disabilities from fully participating in school and community life. Actions may support access to: Inclusive education Recreation Community activities School participation Projects might work directly with schools, communities, local organisations or families to create environments in which children with disabilities can participate alongside their peers. Inclusive Education Inclusive education is one of the clearest intervention areas under this priority. Programmes could potentially focus on: School accessibility Teacher capacity Inclusive teaching Peer support Participation in school life Family-school collaboration Prevention of discrimination The objective should be not only to increase attendance but to improve actual participation and educational inclusion. Addressing Stigma and Harmful Social Norms The call explicitly encourages initiatives addressing: Stigma and discriminatory social norms through: Awareness Community engagement Stigma can limit children even where formal rights exist. For example, negative assumptions may lead communities to believe that children with disabilities: Cannot learn Should remain at home Cannot participate in sport Cannot make decisions Should be treated differently from peers Projects addressing such attitudes should ideally go beyond one-directional awareness campaigns and promote sustained engagement with communities. Peer Interaction and Life Skills The programme also identifies: Peer interaction Life-skills development Self-advocacy as possible areas of action. This recognizes the importance of children developing: Confidence Communication Social relationships Independence Agency Projects may therefore directly support children with disabilities to become active participants rather than passive beneficiaries. Meaningful Participation in Decisions Children with disabilities should also have opportunities to participate in: Decisions affecting them. This may include decisions concerning: Education Services Community activities Programme design Family support The strongest projects may therefore involve children in programme planning, implementation or feedback processes in age- and disability-appropriate ways. Culture, Sport and Social Activities The call additionally identifies: Cultural activities Sports Social activities as important spaces for inclusion. These areas are sometimes overlooked in disability programming even though they are essential for: Friendship Confidence Belonging Personal development Community participation Priority Area 3: Family and Enabling Environment The third priority recognizes that children’s well-being depends heavily on the environments surrounding them. Projects can strengthen: Families Caregivers Communities Local services Social-protection connections Caregiver Training Actions may provide families with training on: Inclusive caregiving. This could include practical knowledge concerning: Supporting children’s development Communication Participation Independence Positive discipline Rights The precise content should reflect the needs of participating children and caregivers. Counselling and Peer Support Networks The call also identifies: Counselling Peer support as possible interventions. Caregivers can experience: Isolation Stress Financial pressure Limited access to information Peer groups can help families: Exchange information Share strategies Access emotional support Connect with services Advocate collectively Community-Based Support and Rehabilitation Eligible activities may include: Practical care assistance Community-rooted rehabilitation This can help ensure children receive support within their families and communities rather than becoming unnecessarily isolated from everyday community life. Improving Accessibility Another major intervention area is the: Physical and social accessibility of community spaces and services. Projects may therefore work on barriers affecting access to: Community centres Schools Health facilities Public services Recreation Social activities Accessibility should be understood broadly. It may involve: Physical design Communication Attitudes Procedures Information formats Connecting Families With Social Protection The programme specifically refers to strengthening connections with existing Egyptian social-protection schemes, including: Takaful Karama supplementary payments for households including persons with disabilities Public health insurance Other available entitlements This makes social-protection navigation an important possible component of a broader disability-inclusion project. Supporting the Economic Resilience of Caregivers The call also permits caregiver economic resilience to be addressed through activities such as: Livelihood programmes Community-based savings groups provided these are integrated into a broader intervention supporting the care and inclusion of children with disabilities. In other words, a standalone livelihood programme would not necessarily meet the programme purpose. Economic resilience should be linked clearly to improved outcomes for: Children Families Inclusion Caregiving Projects Addressing Several Priorities Are Encouraged A proposal is required to address at least: One priority area. However, integrated projects addressing more than one are considered particularly favourably. For example, a project might combine: Child-protection training Inclusive education Parent peer-support groups Social-protection access Local NGO funding Such a model could potentially address all three priority areas in an integrated way. Applicants should nevertheless avoid adding activities simply to appear comprehensive. Every activity should contribute logically to: The problem analysis Objectives Outputs Outcomes Funding Available Detailed call summaries report a total budget of: €3,900,000 for the programme. Individual grants are reported to range from: €650,000 to €1,000,000 per project. These are substantial multi-year grants. Applicants should therefore be capable of managing: Large budgets Partnerships Monitoring Reporting Sub-granting Safeguarding Compliance EU Funding Percentage The detailed call information reports that an EU grant may cover between: 51% and 95% of total eligible costs. Where the grant does not cover 100% of project costs, applicants will need to identify appropriate additional financing in accordance with the official rules. Prospective applicants should consult the official guidelines for: Co-financing rules Eligible sources Budget format Ineligible costs before finalising their financial plan. Project Duration Proposed actions are reported to run for: 24 to 36 months. This makes the programme suitable for interventions requiring enough time to: Build local partnerships Test approaches Strengthen organisations Work with communities Measure changes Institutionalize effective practices Applicants should propose a duration that matches the complexity of their intervention. At Least 60% of Eligible Costs for Financial Support to Third Parties One of the most distinctive elements of the programme is the requirement that a substantial share of funding be passed to smaller or local organisations. Detailed summaries report that at least: 60% of the total eligible costs of the action must be used for: Financial support to third parties. This means the lead applicant is not intended simply to implement a €1 million project itself. A central purpose is to strengthen and resource local actors. Who Could Receive Third-Party Support? Potential third-party recipients may include: Civil society organisations Community-based organisations Organisations of persons with disabilities Other eligible Egyptian nonprofit organisations Detailed call summaries indicate that third-party beneficiaries should be legally established in Egypt and have relevant experience working with or for: Children Children with disabilities Families Communities Maximum Third-Party Grant The normal maximum support to an individual third-party organisation is reported as: €60,000 unless a larger amount is specifically justified. Applicants should therefore think carefully about the structure of their proposed sub-granting mechanism. This may include: Selection criteria Application procedures Due diligence Capacity assessment Grant agreements Monitoring Reporting Safeguarding Technical support Who Can Apply? According to detailed call summaries, eligible lead applicants must be: Nonprofit legal persons established in: Egypt A European Union Member State A contracting party to the European Economic Area Agreement This means the programme is primarily aimed at organisations such as: NGOs Civil society organisations Eligible nonprofit institutions rather than individual applicants. Requirement for an Egyptian Partner Where the lead applicant is not established in Egypt , detailed call information indicates that it must apply with at least: One co-applicant established in Egypt. This partnership requirement reinforces the programme’s emphasis on: Local ownership Egyptian institutional capacity Contextual knowledge Sustainability International organisations should therefore avoid approaching the project as an externally designed intervention delivered in Egypt without meaningful local partnership. Can Individuals Apply? No. This is an organisational call for proposals. It is not intended for: Individual researchers Individual social workers Students Children Parents Individual consultants Individuals may participate in or benefit from funded projects, but they are not the direct grant applicants. Can For-Profit Companies Apply? The detailed eligibility information identifies lead applicants as: Nonprofit legal entities. Therefore, ordinary commercial companies should not be presented as eligible lead applicants unless the full official guidelines provide a specific exception. Geographic Scope All proposed action is intended to take place in: Egypt. This is not a multi-country Middle East or Mediterranean grant. Projects should primarily benefit children with disabilities, families and communities in Egypt. Application Reference The official EU Delegation announcement identifies the call reference as: EuropeAid/186723/DD/ACT/EG. title: Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant 2026: Apply for Up to $249,999 to Expand Workforce Apprenticeship Programs
summary: The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, through the Pennsylvania Department of Labor Industry (L I), has announced the Apprenticeships on the Move: Advancing Pennsylvania’s Workforce Grant , a major workforce development funding opportunity designed to strengthen apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship pathways across the state. Through this Notice of Grant Availability (NGA), approximately $4 million in state funding is available to eligible organizations seeking to develop new Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs or expand existing registered programs in Pennsylvania. Eligible applicants may request up to $249,999 to support projects that respond to employer workforce needs, build stronger talent pipelines, expand access to quality training, address barriers to employment, and create pathways into sustainable careers. The initiative is particularly focused on high-priority sectors including agriculture, energy, life sciences, manufacturing, robotics and technology, education, healthcare, and skilled trades. Applications for the Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant are due by October 2, 2026, at 4:00 PM Eastern Time . The anticipated grant performance period will run from May 1, 2027, through April 30, 2030 . Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant Overview The Apprenticeships on the Move initiative is intended to support Pennsylvania s long-term workforce and economic development objectives by increasing the number, accessibility, and effectiveness of Registered Apprenticeship and Registered Pre-Apprenticeship opportunities. The program recognizes that employers across Pennsylvania are facing increasing demand for skilled workers while also dealing with retirements, workforce shortages, competition for talent, and the loss of institutional knowledge. The grant therefore seeks to fund innovative approaches that connect employers, workforce organizations, education providers, labor organizations, community-based organizations, and other stakeholders to create sustainable workforce pipelines. Under the opportunity, organizations can propose either: Development of a new Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program , or Expansion of an existing Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program. Projects must operate within Pennsylvania and address workforce development needs in one or more of the eligible industry sectors identified by L I. How Much Funding Is Available? Approximately $4,000,000 has been allocated for the Apprenticeships on the Move initiative. Eligible applicants may request: Up to $249,999 per application Funding amounts aligned with the actual scope and needs of the proposed project Funding for eligible activities associated with developing or expanding apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs The exact amount awarded will depend on the funding requested, the quality and competitiveness of applications, available funds, and the evaluation conducted by L I. Pennsylvania may also provide additional funding during the grant period if funds become available through deobligation of other awards. Supplemental funding is not guaranteed and will depend on factors such as grantee performance, demonstrated need, ability to spend additional funds effectively, and continued alignment with the objectives of the grant. The grant is 100% state funded . What Is the Main Purpose of the Apprenticeships on the Move Grant? The central purpose of this grant is to strengthen Pennsylvania s workforce by supporting apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs that respond directly to employer and labor-market needs. The initiative seeks to: Develop new Registered Apprenticeship programs. Develop new Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs. Expand existing registered apprenticeship programs. Expand existing registered pre-apprenticeship programs. Strengthen talent pipelines in high-demand industries. Increase access to apprenticeship opportunities. Help employers address workforce shortages. Provide individuals with skills and workplace experience. Support pathways to industry-recognized credentials. Address barriers preventing individuals from entering apprenticeship pathways. Increase participation among historically underserved and underrepresented populations. Encourage collaboration between employers, education providers, labor organizations, workforce boards, and community organizations. Strengthen Pennsylvania s long-term economic development priorities. Applicants are expected to demonstrate a clear connection between their proposed project and Pennsylvania s workforce and economic development priorities, including Governor Shapiro s Ten-Year Strategic Plan for Economic Development and the Pennsylvania Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) Combined State Plan. Who Can Apply for the Grant? The opportunity is intended for organizations that can serve as sponsors or intermediaries for new or existing registered apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs in Pennsylvania. Eligible organizations may include: Businesses Community-based organizations Economic development organizations Industry associations Labor organizations Local education agencies Local workforce development boards Nonprofit organizations Postsecondary institutions Public libraries STEM ecosystems If an applicant is not the actual program sponsor, the application must provide significant evidence demonstrating that the program sponsor is an involved partner in the proposed project. The organization must also have the capacity to coordinate and manage the project, administer the financial aspects of the grant, collect and report performance information, and work with an evaluator. Two Types of Projects Can Be Funded 1. Development of a New Registered Apprenticeship or Pre-Apprenticeship Program Organizations may apply to establish a new apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program that has not yet been registered at the beginning of the grant performance period. The proposed program must ultimately be registered with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Awardees will have up to one year from the contract start date to finalize registration or demonstrate progress toward registration. Grantees will be expected to establish and maintain communication with representatives of the Pennsylvania Apprenticeship and Training Office (ATO), which serves as the State Apprenticeship Agency (SAA), as they develop and register the program. Organizations that fail to make adequate progress toward registration may have funds deobligated. 2. Expansion of an Existing Registered Program Organizations may also apply to expand an existing Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program that was already registered before the start of the grant performance period. For purposes of this grant, expansion means an increase in the number of participants enrolled in the program . Expansion does not include adding a new occupation to the existing program. Organizations seeking to expand an existing program must ensure that the program sponsor remains compliant with applicable federal and Pennsylvania laws, regulations, policies, standards, and approved program standards. Eligible Industry Sectors The proposed apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program must operate within at least one of the sectors identified by Pennsylvania L I. Eligible sectors are: Agriculture Projects may address workforce needs associated with agricultural occupations and the broader agricultural economy. Energy Programs may develop talent pipelines for energy-related occupations and emerging workforce requirements in the energy sector. Life Sciences Organizations working to develop skilled talent for life sciences industries may submit proposals within this sector. Manufacturing Manufacturing remains a major focus of Pennsylvania s workforce development strategy, and eligible projects may address skills shortages and talent pipeline needs within the sector. Robotics and Technology Programs focused on robotics, technology, and related occupations may qualify where they demonstrate clear workforce demand. Education Education-sector apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship initiatives may be eligible where they respond to identified workforce needs. Healthcare Healthcare workforce development projects may qualify under the healthcare sector. Skilled Trades The skilled trades category includes, but is not limited to: Construction Electrical work HVAC Steamfitting Fiber optics Telecommunications Applicants must identify the applicable sector or sectors in their application and demonstrate how the proposed project addresses workforce development needs within those sectors. Applications proposing programs outside the eligible sectors will be considered ineligible. What Is a Registered Apprenticeship? Registered Apprenticeship is a structured workforce development model that combines employment, training, mentorship, technical education, and recognized credentials. According to the grant announcement, Registered Apprenticeships have five key components: A paid job On-the-job training Related technical instruction Mentorship Credentials This combination allows participants to gain practical work experience while developing technical and occupational skills. For employers, apprenticeship programs can provide a structured way to develop and retain skilled workers. For participants, apprenticeships provide a pathway to earn wages while learning and working toward industry-recognized credentials. What Is a Registered Pre-Apprenticeship? Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs are designed to prepare individuals for entry into Registered Apprenticeship programs. The grant identifies five core components of a registered pre-apprenticeship: An established connection to at least one existing Registered Apprenticeship program. Approved training and curriculum. Hands-on learning through appropriate program designs and approaches. An opportunity to earn an industry-recognized credential. Access to support services and career counseling. Pre-apprenticeship can therefore serve as an important bridge between education, workforce preparation, and formal apprenticeship. Why Is Pennsylvania Investing in Apprenticeships? Pennsylvania is experiencing workforce challenges driven by several factors. Employers are facing shortages of skilled workers, increased competition for talent, and the retirement of experienced workers. As experienced employees leave the workforce, organizations can lose decades of technical knowledge and operational expertise. Registered Apprenticeship programs can help address this challenge by combining experienced-worker mentorship with structured training for new employees. This allows organizations to facilitate knowledge transfer while preparing the next generation of workers. Apprenticeships also provide workers with opportunities to earn wages while acquiring skills and credentials, making them an important pathway into family-sustaining careers. Pennsylvania has historically used apprenticeship models in areas such as construction, manufacturing, and industrial occupations. The Commonwealth is now seeking to expand apprenticeship opportunities into sectors such as healthcare, education, agriculture, energy, life sciences, robotics, technology, and telecommunications. What Should Successful Projects Demonstrate? Applicants must clearly demonstrate that the proposed program responds to a real workforce need. A strong application should provide evidence such as: Labor market information Employer demand Workforce shortage data Talent pipeline gaps Economic development information Information about the occupations being targeted The number of apprentices or pre-apprentices expected to be served Information about the geographic area to be served Evidence of employer involvement Evidence of stakeholder partnerships The applicant must also explain how the project contributes to Pennsylvania s broader workforce and economic development goals. Priority Areas That Can Strengthen an Application The grant provides priority consideration for proposals demonstrating certain characteristics. Previously Unfunded Programs Priority may be given to new initiatives that have not previously received funding, including initiatives developed by existing Registered Apprenticeship or Pre-Apprenticeship sponsors. On-the-Job Learning, Related Technical Instruction and Supportive Services Priority consideration may be given to: Registered Apprenticeship programs using grant funds to support on-the-job learning, related technical instruction, and supportive services. Pre-Apprenticeship programs using grant funds to support paid work experience, related technical instruction, and supportive services. Applicants seeking this priority must reflect the relevant expenses in the applicable budget categories. Group Apprenticeship Models and Multi-County Programs Priority may be given to group Registered Apprenticeship models or pre-apprenticeship programs operating physically across multiple counties. For multi-county pre-apprenticeship replication, the program must have physical operations in at least three counties. Historically Underserved and Underrepresented Populations Applicants are encouraged to develop diverse talent pipelines that expand apprenticeship access for groups that have historically been underrepresented or underserved. These may include: Women People of color Individuals with disabilities Veterans Individuals from underserved or unserved communities Individuals who speak English as a second language Justice-impacted or adjudicated populations Individuals experiencing multiple barriers to employment Applicants should explain how their programs will identify and address barriers to education, training, and employment. Accessibility Priority consideration may also be given to projects that design, create, adjust, or upgrade physical and digital environments and services to improve accessibility for apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship participants. Labor Union Collaboration Applications demonstrating meaningful collaboration with labor unions can receive priority consideration. The labor union must either be the applicant or provide a letter of commitment explaining its specific role in the project. Potential involvement could include: Serving as an affiliated Registered Apprenticeship sponsor. Supporting curriculum development. Supporting a Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program. Providing continuing support after the grant period. Addressing Barriers to Apprenticeship Participation A major component of the opportunity is the expectation that projects address barriers that prevent people from entering or completing apprenticeship pathways. Applicants should consider barriers such as: Transportation challenges Basic skills deficiencies Socioeconomic limitations Program waitlists Program choice restrictions Workplace accessibility challenges Other barriers to education and employment Projects that provide meaningful solutions to these challenges can strengthen access to apprenticeship opportunities. Required Program Outcomes Applicants are expected to propose measurable participant and program outcomes. For new Registered Apprenticeship programs, the desired outcome is that 80% of participants either remain active apprentices or successfully complete the program . For group apprenticeship models, the same 80% target applies to participants. For Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs, applicants must establish targets for completion and transition into the affiliated Registered Apprenticeship program. At least 30% of pre-apprentices who complete the program must matriculate into the affiliated Registered Apprenticeship program . The same 30% matriculation requirement applies to eligible pre-apprenticeship programs being replicated across multiple counties. Expansion projects are similarly expected to focus on participation, completion, retention, and progression into apprenticeship. Performance Metrics L I will work with successful applicants to establish performance metrics during the grant period. Applicants should propose measurable outputs and outcomes covering areas such as: Participant enrollment Participant demographics Continued participation Program completion Employer engagement Training provider engagement Apprentice and pre-apprentice participation Transition from pre-apprenticeship into apprenticeship Credentials obtained Participant wages Program impact Partnership activities Projects should also track the average wage of apprentices at the time of program completion. Grantees are expected to maintain secure, confidential, accurate, and complete participant records for verification and compliance purposes. Grant Evaluation Criteria Applications will be reviewed through an initial eligibility review followed by a merit-based evaluation. To be considered for funding, an application must achieve at least 70% of the total available score, equivalent to 84 out of 120 points . The evaluation structure is: Evaluation Area Points Project Design and Management Plan 25 Performance Outcomes 15 Impact and Sustainability 15 Stakeholder Engagement and Partnership 15 Other Selection Factors/Priority Considerations 35 Budget and Budget Justification 15 Total 120 This scoring structure makes it important for applicants to address every evaluation category directly and provide evidence rather than relying on general descriptions. Project Design and Management Plan This section is worth 25 points . Applicants should clearly explain: The workforce need being addressed. The population to be served. Employers involved. Occupations targeted. Geographic area covered. Relevant labor market information. Employer demand. Workforce shortages. Talent pipeline gaps. The number of apprentices or pre-apprentices to be served. How traditionally underserved populations will be reached. How the project aligns with Pennsylvania s WIOA Combined State Plan. How the project aligns with Pennsylvania s economic development priorities. The implementation timeline. Cohort start and completion dates. Key milestones. Registration steps. Long-term sustainability. Potential for scaling and replication. Applicants must use the required timeline template in Appendix D. Performance Outcomes This category is worth 15 points . Applicants must describe their intended outcomes and explain how those outcomes will be measured. The application should include: Goals Services Expected outcomes Number of people to be served Performance indicators Enrollment targets Completion targets Employer engagement Training provider engagement Participant retention Wage outcomes The Goals and Outcomes Table in Appendix E must be used as required. Impact and Sustainability This category is worth 15 points . Applicants should explain how the project will contribute to the broader goals of the Apprenticeships on the Move initiative. They should identify: Credentials participants will receive. Expected impact on participants. Expected impact on employers. Impact of partnerships. Data tracking and reporting capacity. Recruitment metrics. Participation metrics. Completion and accomplishment metrics. Long-term sustainability. Applicants must also complete the Sustainability Plan in Appendix F. The sustainability strategy should explain how the apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program will continue after the grant period ends. Stakeholder Engagement and Partnerships This section is worth 15 points . Applicants should identify the organizations and stakeholders involved in the proposed project and clearly define their roles. Potential partners may include: Employers Workforce development organizations Educational institutions Community-based organizations Labor organizations Economic development organizations Workforce boards Training providers Applications should explain the responsibilities of each partner and demonstrate that the applicant has the capacity to coordinate the partnership effectively. Key personnel should also be identified by name, along with their roles and contributions to the project. Sector Diversity Pennsylvania is also seeking diversity among funded sectors. No more than three awards may be made to applications supporting the same industry sector , even where projects serve different geographic areas. Applicants should therefore clearly identify the sector or sectors their project supports and explain how their proposal responds to workforce needs in that sector. Budget Requirements The proposed budget must be directly connected to the project narrative. Applicants should provide: Detailed budget line items. Requested funds. Leveraged funds. Costs by category. Quantities. Unit costs where applicable. Detailed justification for expenditures. Explanation of how expenditures support project activities and deliverables. Costs that are not discussed in the proposal should not appear in the budget. Administrative costs may not exceed 10% of the total amount requested . The budget must cover the entire performance period from May 1, 2027, to April 30, 2030 . Reimbursement-Based Funding Applicants should understand that this grant does not operate as an upfront lump-sum payment. Grant expenses are reimbursed after they have been incurred and documented. Monthly invoices must be supported by appropriate documentation. Organizations should therefore have sufficient financial and administrative capacity to manage expenses, maintain records, and submit invoices properly. Awardees must document expenses consistently with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. Supporting documentation may include evidence such as: Invoices Competitive bidding documentation Time records Payroll documentation Other appropriate expenditure records Employee time charged to the grant must accurately reflect the actual amount of time spent working on grant activities. Important Restriction for New Programs Organizations developing new Registered Apprenticeship or Pre-Apprenticeship programs should pay particular attention to the registration requirement. New programs cannot invoice for: On-the-Job Training (OJT) Related Technical Instruction (RTI) Supportive services before the new apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program has been approved. These expenses must be incurred after program approval. Pennsylvania SAP Vendor Identification Number Applicants are required to have a Pennsylvania SAP Vendor Identification Number . The number can be obtained at no cost through the applicable Pennsylvania vendor registration process. Applicants should begin this process early because obtaining the vendor number may take up to two weeks. An organization may submit its application before receiving the number if necessary, but a grant will not be awarded without documentation of the required Pennsylvania Vendor Identification Number. Applicants unable to meet this requirement at the time of award may have to relinquish the award. Fiscal Agent Requirements A fiscal agent is an organization that accepts responsibility for managing grant funds on behalf of the grantee. The fiscal agent may be a business, school, workforce organization, or another eligible organization capable of managing the financial requirements of the award. The fiscal agent is responsible for areas such as: Fiscal accounting Invoicing Payments State and federal tax reporting Financial documentation Audit requirements A fiscal agent must also obtain employee dishonesty/theft insurance of at least $100,000 . Organizations that can manage the fiscal responsibilities themselves may serve as their own fiscal agents. Where Local Workforce Development Boards apply as a region, the region must designate a single LWDB as the lead applicant and fiscal agent. Application Package Requirements Applicants must download and complete the official application documents provided by Pennsylvania L I. The application package must include several components. 1. Application Form The Application Form must: Be completed in full. Be no more than one page. Be saved as a single file. Follow the required naming convention: ApplicantName_App_Form . 2. Project Summary Cover The Project Summary Cover must not exceed three pages. It should include: Applicant name Fiscal agent name Vendor ID number Unique Entity Identifier, where applicable Project title Project county Project service area Municipality House and Senate districts served Project partners Brief project summary Project point of contact Contact information 3. Project Narrative The Project Narrative is a central part of the application and may be up to 10 pages , excluding the Goals/Outcomes Table, Timeline, and Sustainability Plan attachments. The narrative should address: Project Design and Management Plan Project steps Performance Outcomes Impact and Sustainability Stakeholder Engagement and Partnership Other Selection Factors and Priority Considerations Applicants should structure the narrative so that evaluators can easily identify how each evaluation criterion has been addressed. 4. Timeline Applicants must complete the required timeline template. The timeline should show: Implementation steps Dates Milestones Cohort schedules Registration activities ATO engagement Expected outcomes Key benchmarks For new programs, the timeline should specifically demonstrate the steps toward registration. 5. Goals and Outcomes Table Applicants must complete the Goals and Outcomes Table in Appendix E. The table should clearly identify the project s goals, services, participant targets, and expected outcomes. 6. Sustainability Plan Applicants must submit a sustainability plan explaining how the apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program will continue after the grant ends. The plan should demonstrate that the project is designed for long-term impact rather than temporary implementation. 7. Letters of Support Applicants must submit one to three unique letters of support . Letters should demonstrate meaningful partner commitment and strong cross-sector collaboration. They should describe: The partner s role. Responsibilities. Nature of the commitment. How the organization will contribute to project implementation. Applicants are encouraged to establish partnerships across areas such as education, workforce development, business, economic development, and community services. 8. Grant Financial Reporting Package The Grant Financial Reporting Package must be submitted as a single Excel file. It should include: Requested funds Leveraged funds Expenditures by category Line items Budget justification The budget will form the financial basis for the grant and reimbursement payments. 9. Local Workforce Development Board Notification Applicants that are not LWDBs must notify their regional Local Workforce Development Board of their application. A copy of the notification email must be included in the application package. The requirement does not apply to LWDB applicants. 10. Worker Protection Certification Applicants must complete the EO 2021-06 Worker Protection Certification Form. The certification relates to compliance with Pennsylvania s: Unemployment Compensation Law Workers Compensation Law State labor laws Workforce safety laws Application Formatting Requirements Applications must follow the required formatting specifications. The main application documents should be: Single-spaced 8.5 by 11 inches Formatted with one-inch margins Written in 11-point Calibri font Submitted as PDF files, except for the Budget Form Numbered with page numbers in the footer Applications may not contain hyperlinks. Applicants must also ensure that they do not include proprietary or sensitive business information. Incomplete applications or applications that fail to meet the specified requirements will not be reviewed or scored. Evaluators will review only the specified number of pages even if an application exceeds the permitted length. Letters of Support and the Budget Form do not count toward the applicable page limit. How to Submit the Application Completed application packages must be submitted electronically by email to the Pennsylvania Apprenticeship and Training Office Grants resource account: ATOGrants@pa.gov The application must be submitted no later than: October 2, 2026, at 4:00 PM ET Late applications will not be accepted. Applicants should ensure that the email subject line follows the required grant naming instructions. The Notice specifies the application subject as: “Apprenticeships on the Move: Advancing Pennsylvania’s Workforce” Applicants should retain the automatic email confirmation received after submission. If an applicant does not receive the automatic response, the applicant should forward the sent email to the ATO Grants Resource Account and provide the grant name, submission date and time, name, and telephone number. Applicants may also contact the L I Apprenticeship and Training Office at (717) 787-6997 if they do not receive an automatic confirmation. Important Grant Timeline Applicants should take note of the following dates: August 12, 2026: Notice of Grant Availability released. August 26, 2026 at 9:00 AM ET: Bidder s Conference. September 8, 2026 at 4:00 PM ET: Deadline for submitting questions. October 2, 2026 at 4:00 PM ET: Application deadline. May 1, 2027: Anticipated performance period start. April 30, 2030: Anticipated contract end date. Questions must be submitted to ATOGrants@pa.gov with the subject line “Question- Apprenticeships on the Move.” Questions submitted after the deadline will not be answered. Grant Award and Notification Process Funding will be awarded competitively based on the availability of funds and the quality of submitted applications. L I expects to notify applicants by email within 30 days following the award determination . Applicants whose proposals are not selected may request a feedback call within 30 days of receiving their denial notification. Feedback requests must be submitted by the authorized representative using the appropriate email subject line. Successful applicants will be required to enter into a Workforce Grant Agreement with L I unless they already have an applicable grant agreement in place. Reporting and Monitoring Requirements Successful grantees will have substantial reporting responsibilities. Grantees will be required to submit program and fiscal progress reports: Monthly Annually At the conclusion of the project Final closeout reports must generally be submitted within 60 days after the end of the performance period , or within 60 days of full expenditure, whichever occurs first. Grantees may also be required to: Participate in routine calls with L I. Share project progress. Discuss best practices. Receive technical assistance. Participate in third-party evaluation. Collect participant information. Maintain appropriate records. Submit additional performance data when requested. Organizations must ensure that personally identifiable information is adequately protected and handled in accordance with applicable Commonwealth data protection requirements. Allowable and Unallowable Costs Grant funds must support the objectives and activities of the Apprenticeships on the Move initiative. Allowable costs may include eligible project activities and administrative costs, subject to the grant requirements. Administrative costs may not exceed 10% of the amount requested . Examples of unallowable costs include: Pre-award costs Building construction Lobbying services Costs unrelated to direct performance of the award Other expenses not aligned with the approved grant proposal Pre-award costs are incurred at the applicant s own risk and will not be reimbursed. L I can also disallow expenses that do not align with the approved grant proposal or Notice of Grant Award. How Applicants Can Strengthen Their Proposals Because the grant uses a competitive merit-based evaluation, applicants should develop their proposals around the scoring criteria rather than simply describing their organization. A strong proposal should: Clearly identify a genuine workforce problem. Support the problem statement with labor-market and employer-demand evidence. Identify the specific occupations and sector being targeted. Clearly define the population and geographic area to be served. Demonstrate meaningful employer participation. Build strong cross-sector partnerships. Explain how the project will increase apprenticeship participation. Address barriers to entry and completion. Establish measurable participant targets. Provide realistic completion and retention goals. Demonstrate a clear pathway from pre-apprenticeship into Registered Apprenticeship where applicable. Explain how participants will obtain credentials. Provide a detailed implementation timeline. Demonstrate a credible path toward program registration where a new program is proposed. Include a realistic and well-justified budget. Demonstrate long-term sustainability. Explain how project data will be collected, protected, analyzed, and reported. Address priority considerations wherever applicable. Secure strong letters of support from committed partners. Ensure every required application component is complete and correctly formatted. Key Considerations for New Apprenticeship Programs Organizations proposing new programs should begin registration-related planning early. The application should explain: The occupation to be supported. Why the occupation is appropriate for apprenticeship. The workforce need. Employer demand. Proposed training structure. Related technical instruction. On-the-job learning. Mentorship. Credentials. Program partners. Registration milestones. Engagement with the Apprenticeship and Training Office. Applicants should verify whether their proposed occupation is apprenticeable through the relevant apprenticeship resources. If an occupation is not already recognized as apprenticeable, applicants should use the applicable apprenticeability process and ensure compliance with Pennsylvania apprenticeship requirements. Long-Term Sustainability Sustainability is a major part of the evaluation. Applicants must explain how the program will continue after the grant period. A credible sustainability plan could demonstrate how partnerships, employer participation, training infrastructure, funding sources, program operations, and participant recruitment will continue beyond the grant. The objective is to establish apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship systems that remain useful to employers and workers after grant funding has ended. Why This Grant Matters for Pennsylvania s Workforce The Apprenticeships on the Move initiative represents an effort to connect workforce development directly with employer demand. Instead of treating workforce training as a standalone activity, the initiative encourages collaboration among businesses, educational institutions, workforce boards, community organizations, labor organizations, and other stakeholders. By combining paid work experience, technical instruction, mentorship, support services, and recognized credentials, apprenticeship programs can help individuals transition into skilled occupations while giving employers a structured mechanism for developing talent. The initiative also places significant emphasis on expanding access for populations that have historically experienced barriers to employment and apprenticeship participation. Visit HERE to learn more about the Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant 2026. Conclusion The Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move: Advancing Pennsylvania s Workforce Grant provides a significant opportunity for organizations across Pennsylvania to develop and expand Registered Apprenticeship and Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs. With approximately $4 million available and individual applicants able to request up to $249,999 , the initiative is designed to support projects that address workforce shortages, strengthen talent pipelines, expand access to quality careers, and align workforce development with Pennsylvania s economic priorities.
